title: CE361: Theory of Structures
description: Analysis of determinate structures: trusses, loads, beams, shear and moment, determinacy and stability.

topics.title: Reactions to Determinate Structures  -  Trusses
topics.description: Reviewer on trusses, zero-force members, method of joints, and method of sections.

content.text: A truss is made of slender members connected at their ends by pins. Ideally, members carry only axial forces and each member is either in tension or compression.

items: Tension - The member is being pulled.
Compression - The member is being pushed.
Pin support - Usually provides horizontal and vertical reactions, Ax and Ay.
Roller support - Usually provides one vertical reaction, By.

content.text: For the whole truss: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, and ΣM = 0.
Zero-force members carry no axial load for the given loading condition. They can be identified by inspecting an unloaded joint.

content.alt: Truss showing zero-force members
content.caption: Zero-force members marked with red X symbols

content.alt: Second truss zero-force member example
content.caption: Zero-force member identification at unloaded joints

content.alt: Large truss zero-force member example
content.caption: Zero-force members in a loaded truss

content.alt: Supported truss zero-force member example
content.caption: Zero-force member locations in a multi-panel truss

items: Rule 1: If a joint has only two non-collinear members and no load or support reaction, both members are zero-force members.
Rule 2: If a joint has three members, two collinear and one non-collinear, with no external load at the joint, the non-collinear member is a zero-force member.

content.text: The method of joints analyzes one joint at a time. At every joint, use ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.

items: Determine the support reactions.
Identify zero-force members.
Start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces.
Assume all unknown members are in tension.
Resolve diagonal forces into horizontal and vertical components.
Solve using ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.
A positive answer indicates tension; a negative answer indicates compression.

content.alt: Method of joints worked example
content.caption: Method of joints example with a 500 N load

content.text: For the illustrated 45-degree example, the diagonal member is 707.1 N compression, the vertical member is 500 N tension, and the horizontal member is 500 N tension.
For a diagonal member at angle θ, resolve its force into components: Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ.

items: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse
cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse
For a 3-4-5 triangle: sin θ = 3/5 and cos θ = 4/5.

content.text: Always draw the free-body diagram first, then assign the correct signs to the horizontal and vertical components.
The method of sections is useful when only a few member forces are required. An imaginary cut is passed through the truss, normally through no more than three unknown members.

content.alt: Method of sections truss example
content.caption: A section cut through a truss

content.alt: Method of sections example with marked members
content.caption: Members GH, HC, and BC selected for analysis

content.alt: Moment points for method of sections
content.caption: Choosing moment centers to solve selected member forces

content.alt: Another method of sections example
content.caption: Section cut through BF, BC, and FG

content.alt: Moment analysis for method of sections
content.caption: Moment equations used to solve selected members

items: Pass the cut through the required members.
Isolate the simpler side of the truss.
Use ΣM = 0 first when possible.
Then use ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.
Take moments about a point where two unknown cut-member forces intersect to eliminate them.

content.alt: Method of joints seatwork problem
content.caption: Seatwork problem: determine FG, DG, and CD

content.text: For seatwork problems, begin by finding the support reactions for the entire truss. Then select a joint with no more than two unknown member forces and proceed joint by joint.

items: Identify all joints, members, supports, and external loads.
Check dimensions and angles.
Search for zero-force members.
Use the entire truss to calculate support reactions.
For the method of joints, use ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.
For the method of sections, use ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, and ΣM = 0.
Label every final result as tension, compression, or zero-force.

content.text: Sign convention: A positive result means the assumed tension direction is correct. A negative result means the member is in compression.

topics.title: Types of Structures and Loads
topics.description: Reviewer on structural systems, load classifications, load transfer, and NSCP 2015 load combinations.

content.text: A structure is an assembly of connected members designed to support loads safely and transfer them to the ground. Structural design must provide adequate strength, stability, and serviceability.

items: Strength - The structure resists failure or collapse.
Stability - The structure maintains equilibrium under applied loads.
Serviceability - Deflection, vibration, and cracking remain within acceptable limits.
Durability - Materials and connections perform for the intended service life.

content.text: Structures may be classified by their form, material, or the way their members carry forces.

items: Frame structures use beams, columns, and connections to resist gravity and lateral loads.
Trusses use straight members connected at joints; ideal members carry mainly axial tension or compression.
Arches carry loads primarily through compression along a curved form.
Cables and membranes carry tension and are shaped by the applied loading.
Shells and plates distribute loads across thin, curved or flat surfaces.
Mass structures resist loads through their own weight and bulk, as in dams or retaining structures.

content.text: Different members are arranged so that each carries the internal action for which it is most suitable.

items: Slabs span across spaces and transfer floor or roof loads to beams.
Beams resist bending and shear and transfer loads to girders or columns.
Girders are primary beams that collect loads from smaller beams.
Columns carry mainly axial compression and transfer loads toward the foundation.
Foundations spread structural loads into the supporting soil or rock.
Braces and shear walls resist lateral forces and help maintain stability.

content.text: In a typical building, gravity loads follow a continuous path from the occupied spaces to the ground. The load-transfer sequence is slab -> beams -> girders -> columns -> footings -> soil.

content.alt: Building load transfer from slab to footings
content.caption: Typical gravity-load path through a building

items: Every connection in the load path must be strong and properly detailed.
The supporting member must be checked for the accumulated load it receives.
Foundations distribute reactions so that soil pressure remains safe and acceptable.

content.text: Dead load is the permanent load caused by the self-weight of structural and permanently attached nonstructural components.

items: Beams, slabs, columns, walls, stairs, and foundations
Roofing, floor finishes, ceilings, partitions, and fixed equipment
The self-weight of a member should be included when calculating its design load

content.text: Dead loads are usually calculated from the material density multiplied by the member volume, or from a published unit weight multiplied by the area or length supported.
Live loads are movable or changing loads produced by occupants, furniture, stored materials, vehicles, and similar use. Environmental loads come from natural conditions and site effects.

items: Live load - Occupants, furniture, movable partitions, storage, and vehicles.
Wind load - Pressure or suction caused by wind acting on exposed surfaces.
Earthquake load - Inertial forces generated by ground motion.
Snow or rain load - Accumulation on roofs where applicable.
Temperature load - Expansion or contraction caused by temperature change.
Soil and fluid loads - Lateral pressure, buoyancy, and hydrostatic effects.

content.text: Applied loads create internal forces and deformations. Structural analysis determines the reactions, shear forces, bending moments, axial forces, and torsion required for design.

items: Axial force acts along the member length and may produce tension or compression.
Shear force acts transverse to the member and tends to slide one part past another.
Bending moment causes curvature and bending stress.
Torsion twists a member about its longitudinal axis.

content.text: For a structure in static equilibrium, use the conditions sum of horizontal forces = 0, sum of vertical forces = 0, and sum of moments = 0.

Design load combinations account for the possibility that different loads act together. The National Structural Code of the Philippines (NSCP) 2015 provides separate combinations for strength design using LRFD and for allowable stress design using ASD.

content.alt: NSCP 2015 LRFD and ASD load combinations
content.caption: NSCP 2015 load-combination reference

items: D = dead load
L = live load
W = wind load
E = earthquake load
LRFD applies load factors to produce factored design effects.
ASD compares service-level effects with allowable strengths.
Identify the structural system and its supports.
Trace the complete load path from each load to the foundation.
Classify all applicable dead, live, wind, earthquake, soil, fluid, and temperature loads.
Calculate support reactions and member force effects.
Apply the governing NSCP 2015 LRFD or ASD load combinations.
Check strength, stability, serviceability, and foundation bearing conditions.
Confirm that connections and load-transfer details are continuous and adequate.

content.text: A safe design is not based on one member alone: every member, connection, support, and foundation in the load path must work together.

topics.title: Reactions to Determinate Structures (Beams)
topics.description: Reviewer on load transmission, slabs, tributary loadings, beam internal forces, sign conventions, and shear-and-moment diagrams.

content.text: Gravity loads travel through a continuous structural path. The typical sequence is slab -> beams -> girders -> columns -> footings -> soil.

content.alt: Structural load transmission from slab to foundation
content.caption: Typical load path in a single-storey building

items: Slabs receive floor or roof surface loads.
Beams collect slab loads and transfer them to girders.
Girders support beams and transfer their reactions to columns.
Columns carry the accumulated loads downward.
Footings spread column loads into the supporting ground.

content.text: A one-way slab is designed to span primarily in one direction. A two-way slab spans and distributes load in both directions.

content.alt: Comparison of one-way and two-way slab load paths
content.caption: One-way and two-way slab action

content.text: Let S be the shorter span and L be the longer span. A common classification rule is S/L <= 0.5 for one-way action and S/L > 0.5 for two-way action.

content.alt: Plan showing one-way and two-way slab panels
content.caption: Slab classification using the shorter-to-longer span ratio

content.text: Tributary loading determines how a surface load from a wall, floor, or roof is assigned to the structural members supporting it. The tributary area of a member is the portion of the surface whose load is carried by that member.

items: For an interior member, the tributary width is commonly half the spacing to the adjacent member on each side.
For an exterior member, the tributary area extends from the edge to the midpoint toward the adjacent member.
A surface load in kPa multiplied by tributary width in m produces a line load in kN/m.
Tributary areas can be traced for beams, girders, and columns.

content.alt: Structural grid used to identify tributary areas
content.caption: Beam, girder, and column locations on a structural grid

content.alt: Tributary areas of beams
content.caption: Typical tributary areas for exterior and interior beams

content.alt: Tributary areas of girders
content.caption: Typical tributary areas for girders

content.text: For a floor carrying a uniformly distributed surface load, first determine the tributary area of each member. Multiply the surface load by the tributary area to obtain the total load delivered to that member, then use equilibrium to determine its reactions.

content.alt: Example of a floor slab supported by floor beams and a girder
content.caption: Floor slab load transferred through floor beams to a girder

content.text: Internal forces are the stress resultants that develop inside a member when external loads act on it. They are found by making a section cut and applying equilibrium to one part of the member.

items: Axial force N acts along the member's longitudinal axis.
Shear force V acts perpendicular to the member's axis.
Bending moment M causes the member to curve.
Ideal truss members are subjected only to axial forces, while beams and rigid-frame members may carry axial force, shear, and bending moment.

content.alt: Internal axial, shear, and bending forces in a beam
content.caption: Internal force resultants exposed by a section cut

content.alt: Internal forces in a frame member
content.caption: Internal forces in a rigid frame

content.text: Use one consistent sign convention when calculating internal forces. In the convention shown in the lecture, positive axial force is tension and positive bending moment produces a sagging or smiling shape.

items: Axial force: (+) tension; (-) compression.
Shear force: (+) left side up and right side down; (-) left side down and right side up.
Bending moment: (+) sagging or smile; (-) hogging or sad shape.

content.alt: Sign convention diagrams for axial force, shear force, and bending moment
content.caption: Positive and negative internal-force conventions

content.text: Shear and moment diagrams graphically show how internal forces vary along a beam. They help identify critical regions so that member size, material, and reinforcement can be selected appropriately.

items: A point load causes a sudden jump in the shear diagram.
A distributed load causes the shear diagram to vary continuously.
The slope of the moment diagram is related to the shear force.
The maximum or minimum bending moment occurs where shear is zero or changes sign.
At a simple support with no applied couple, the beam-end moment is usually zero.

content.alt: Example shear and moment diagrams for a beam
content.caption: Shear and moment diagrams under concentrated loads

content.alt: Beam loading examples for shear and moment analysis
content.caption: Beam loading cases used for internal-force analysis

content.text: A statically determinate beam can be solved using the three planar equilibrium equations: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, and ΣM = 0. Replace distributed loads with equivalent resultant forces acting at their centroids before solving reactions.

items: A pin support can provide horizontal and vertical reactions.
A roller support generally provides one reaction normal to the supporting surface.
The resultant of a uniform distributed load acts at the midpoint of its loaded length.
The resultant of a triangular distributed load acts one-third of the base length from the larger-intensity end, or two-thirds from the zero-intensity end.
After solving reactions, check force and moment equilibrium.

content.alt: Free-body diagrams for beam internal force analysis
content.caption: Free-body diagrams for sections of a loaded beam

content.text: Practice determining the internal shear and moment at a point 1.5 ft to the left of point C. Also determine the internal shear and moment at a point 2 m to the left of the roller support. Begin by finding the support reactions, then isolate the portion of the beam containing the section.

items: Draw the complete free-body diagram.
Replace distributed loads with equivalent resultants.
Solve the support reactions using equilibrium.
Cut the beam at the requested point.
Apply the selected sign convention to solve V and M.

topics.title: Determinacy of Structures
topics.description: Reviewer on support reactions, structural stability, static determinacy, degree of indeterminacy, and truss determinacy.

content.text: A support restricts one or more movements of a structure and develops reaction forces or moments. The number and direction of the reactions depend on the support type.

content.alt: Light cable, link, roller, rocker, and smooth-contact support reactions
content.caption: Support types with one unknown reaction

items: Cable or link - The reaction acts along the cable or link.
Roller or rocker - The reaction acts perpendicular to the contact surface.
Smooth contacting surface - The reaction is normal to the surface.

content.alt: Pin, slider, fixed-connected collar, and fixed support reactions
content.caption: Support types with two or three unknown reactions

items: Pin or hinge - Provides two force components, usually Ax and Ay.
Slider or fixed-connected collar - Can provide force components and, when rotation is restrained, a moment.
Fixed support - Provides horizontal force, vertical force, and a reaction moment.

content.text: A structure is stable when its supports and members prevent rigid-body motion and maintain a reliable load path. Stability must be checked both externally, through the support arrangement, and internally, through the member arrangement.

content.alt: Beam with support arrangement illustrating external stability
content.caption: External stability depends on the support arrangement

content.alt: Examples of externally stable and unstable support arrangements
content.caption: Examples of external stability and instability

content.alt: Examples of internally stable and unstable member arrangements
content.caption: Internal stability depends on the member geometry and connections

items: External instability occurs when the reactions cannot prevent translation or rotation of the entire structure.
Internal instability occurs when the members can move relative to one another even though the external supports appear adequate.
A structure can be externally stable but internally unstable, so both checks are necessary.

content.text: For a stable planar structure, the basic comparison is between the number of unknown reactions R and the number of independent equilibrium equations 3m, where m is the number of rigid bodies or members being considered.

content.alt: Criteria comparing reactions and equilibrium equations
content.caption: General determinacy criteria for structures

items: R = 3m - The structure is statically determinate if it is also stable.
R > 3m - The structure is statically indeterminate; extra reactions require additional compatibility or deformation equations.
R < 3m - The structure is unstable or has insufficient constraints.

content.text: The degree of static indeterminacy is the number of redundant unknowns beyond the available equilibrium equations. For the general case, DI = R - 3m.

content.alt: Examples of stable, determinate, and indeterminate structures
content.caption: Examples classified by stability and degree of indeterminacy

content.text: For a planar truss, use the number of members m, external reactions R, and joints j. The truss determinacy relationship is m + R = 2j.

content.alt: Truss determinacy criteria and degree of indeterminacy equation
content.caption: Determinacy criteria for planar trusses

items: m + R = 2j - The truss is statically determinate if it is stable and properly arranged.
m + R > 2j - The truss is statically indeterminate.
m + R < 2j - The truss is unstable.
For a planar truss, the degree of indeterminacy is DI = m + R - 2j.

content.text: The count is only a necessary condition. A truss that satisfies the numerical equation can still be unstable if its members and joints form a mechanism, so geometry and support conditions must also be inspected.

content.alt: Examples of determinate, indeterminate, and unstable trusses
content.caption: Truss examples classified using member, reaction, and joint counts

items: Step 1: Identify the support types and count every independent reaction component.
Step 2: Check external stability by asking whether the reactions prevent translation and rotation.
Step 3: Check internal stability by inspecting member geometry, hinges, and possible mechanisms.
Step 4: Count the rigid bodies or members and compare R with 3m for a general planar structure.
Step 5: For a planar truss, count members, reactions, and joints and compare m + R with 2j.
Step 6: Compute the degree of indeterminacy only after confirming that the structure is stable.

content.text: A numerical count identifies the likely classification, but it does not replace a stability check. Always confirm that the structure has a continuous and geometrically stable load path.

content.text: Use one consistent sign convention when calculating internal forces. In the convention shown in the lecture, positive axial force is tension and positive bending moment produces a sagging or smiling shape.

items: Axial force: (+) tension; (-) compression.
Shear force: (+) left side up and right side down; (-) left side down and right side up.
Bending moment: (+) sagging or smile; (-) hogging or sad shape.

content.alt: Sign convention diagrams for axial force, shear force, and bending moment
content.caption: Positive and negative internal-force conventions

content.text: Shear and moment diagrams graphically show how internal forces vary along a beam. They help identify critical regions so that member size, material, and reinforcement can be selected appropriately.

items: A point load causes a sudden jump in the shear diagram.
A distributed load causes the shear diagram to vary continuously.
The slope of the moment diagram is related to the shear force.
The maximum or minimum bending moment occurs where shear is zero or changes sign.
At a simple support with no applied couple, the beam-end moment is usually zero.

content.caption: Shear and moment diagrams under concentrated loads

content.text: A statically determinate beam can be solved using the three planar equilibrium equations: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, and ΣM = 0. Replace distributed loads with equivalent resultant forces acting at their centroids before solving reactions.

items: A pin support can provide horizontal and vertical reactions.
A roller support generally provides one reaction normal to the supporting surface.
The resultant of a uniform distributed load acts at the midpoint of its loaded length.
The resultant of a triangular distributed load acts one-third of the base length from the larger-intensity end, or two-thirds from the zero-intensity end.
After solving reactions, check force and moment equilibrium.

Also determine the internal shear and moment at a point 2 m to the left of the roller support. Begin by finding the support reactions, then isolate the portion of the beam containing the section.

items: Draw the complete free-body diagram.

content.text: A support restricts one or more movements of a structure and develops reaction forces or moments. The number and direction of the reactions depend on the support type.

content.alt: Light cable, link, roller, rocker, and smooth-contact support reactions
content.caption: Support types with one unknown reaction

items: Cable or link - The reaction acts along the cable or link.
Roller or rocker - The reaction acts perpendicular to the contact surface.
Smooth contacting surface - The reaction is normal to the surface.

content.alt: Pin, slider, fixed-connected collar, and fixed support reactions
content.caption: Support types with two or three unknown reactions

items: Pin or hinge - Provides two force components, usually Ax and Ay.
Slider or fixed-connected collar - Can provide force components and, when rotation is restrained, a moment.
Fixed support - Provides horizontal force, vertical force, and a reaction moment.

content.text: A structure is stable when its supports and members prevent rigid-body motion and maintain a reliable load path. Stability must be checked both externally, through the support arrangement, and internally, through the member arrangement.

content.alt: Beam with support arrangement illustrating external stability
content.caption: External stability depends on the support arrangement

content.alt: Examples of externally stable and unstable support arrangements
content.caption: Examples of external stability and instability

content.alt: Examples of internally stable and unstable member arrangements
content.caption: Internal stability depends on the member geometry and connections

items: External instability occurs when the reactions cannot prevent translation or rotation of the entire structure.
Internal instability occurs when the members can move relative to one another even though the external supports appear adequate.
A structure can be externally stable but internally unstable, so both checks are necessary.

content.text: For a stable planar structure, the basic comparison is between the number of unknown reactions R and the number of independent equilibrium equations 3m, where m is the number of rigid bodies or members being considered.

content.alt: Criteria comparing reactions and equilibrium equations
content.caption: General determinacy criteria for structures

items: R = 3m - The structure is statically determinate if it is also stable.
R > 3m - The structure is statically indeterminate; extra reactions require additional compatibility or deformation equations.
R < 3m - The structure is unstable or has insufficient constraints.

content.text: The degree of static indeterminacy is the number of redundant unknowns beyond the available equilibrium equations. For the general case, DI = R - 3m.

content.alt: Examples of stable, determinate, and indeterminate structures
content.caption: Examples classified by stability and degree of indeterminacy

content.text: For a planar truss, use the number of members m, external reactions R, and joints j. The truss determinacy relationship is m + R = 2j.

content.alt: Truss determinacy criteria and degree of indeterminacy equation
content.caption: Determinacy criteria for planar trusses

items: m + R = 2j - The truss is statically determinate if it is stable and properly arranged.
m + R > 2j - The truss is statically indeterminate.
m + R < 2j - The truss is unstable.
For a planar truss, the degree of indeterminacy is DI = m + R - 2j.

content.text: The count is only a necessary condition. A truss that satisfies the numerical equation can still be unstable if its members and joints form a mechanism, so geometry and support conditions must also be inspected.

content.alt: Examples of determinate, indeterminate, and unstable trusses
content.caption: Truss examples classified using member, reaction, and joint counts

items: Step 1: Identify the support types and count every independent reaction component.
Step 2: Check external stability by asking whether the reactions prevent translation and rotation.
Step 3: Check internal stability by inspecting member geometry, hinges, and possible mechanisms.
Step 4: Count the rigid bodies or members and compare R with 3m for a general planar structure.
Step 5: For a planar truss, count members, reactions, and joints and compare m + R with 2j.
Step 6: Compute the degree of indeterminacy only after confirming that the structure is stable.

content.text: A numerical count identifies the likely classification, but it does not replace a stability check. Always confirm that the structure has a continuous and geometrically stable load path.
